draft.title: Bush foods and changed biomes
card: Bush foods are native plants and animals that First Nations Australians have eaten for thousands of years. They grew in biomes that people understood and cared for.
Clearing land and grazing livestock changed those biomes. Some bush foods became much less common as a result.
The yam daisy (myrrnong) is one example. It was a root food in Victoria, and grazing animals ate it and damaged the grasslands where it grew.
Some bush foods are now grown on farms and sold. This gives people more ways to get food, and it can bring income to the people who grow it.
draft.remember: Changing a biome can reduce the foods it holds, and some bush foods are now grown and sold.

a.q: Why did the yam daisy (myrrnong) become less common in Victoria?
opts: Clearing and grazing changed the grasslands where it grew
People stopped eating it, so it was no longer planted
Bush foods can only grow where there are no grasslands
Farms began to grow it and sell it across Victoria
a.why: Clearing land and grazing livestock changed the grasslands the yam daisy grew in, and animals ate and damaged it. Growing and selling bush foods is a separate, later change and does not explain why the plant became less common.
a.clue: Think about what happened to the land where it grew.

b.q: A farm in Victoria grows native bush foods and sells them to local shops. What does this show about bush foods?
opts: Some bush foods are now grown and sold
All bush foods are now common in the wild
Bush foods are no longer part of any biome
Grazing has made bush foods easier to find
b.why: The farm grows bush foods and sells them, so some bush foods are now grown and sold. The farm does not show that wild bush foods have recovered. Clearing and grazing reduced many of them.
b.clue: Look at what the farm does with the plants.

a.best: Clearing and grazing changed the grasslands where it grew

b.best: Some bush foods are now grown and sold

problems.detail: The stem already says the farm grows and sells bush foods, and the right option restates this almost word for word. It is also the only option with the softer qualifier 'Some', while the others use 'All', 'no longer any' or plainly false claims. A student can pick it without understanding the idea.

check.summary: The facts on the card and the answers to both questions are sound. Question b gives its answer away, because the stem restates the right option and the distractors are plainly false.

b.q: Kai studies two grasslands in Victoria. One has been fenced off from sheep for many years, and the other is grazed. Where is he more likely to find yam daisy?
opts: The fenced area, because sheep have not eaten it there
The grazed area, because sheep spread its seeds
Either area, because grazing does not affect it
Neither area, because it now grows only on farms
b.why: Grazing animals ate the yam daisy and damaged the grasslands where it grew, so the area kept free of sheep is more likely to still have it. Grazing did not help the plant spread, and it still grows in grasslands, not only on farms.
b.clue: Think about what grazing animals did to the yam daisy.
